title: The day the plan should turn
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; no doses or infusion rates are given. Local protocol and the attending nephrologist’s judgment come first.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on duty at a provincial hospital in Pangasinan. At 22:10 on Sunday, Mr. Rodolfo Agustin, 63, a rice farmer with hypertension, is brought to the emergency room with three days of cough and fever. His chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe pneumonia. His blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, his pulse 118, his hands cold, his capillary refill 4 seconds, and he is confused. His creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. The ward has no bed scale; his daughter thinks he weighed about 60 kg last month.

The intern, Dr. Bea Soriano, will follow him on the ward. The nephrology fellow, Dr. Ramon Ilagan, covers the hospital, and the attending nephrologist takes calls.

n1.prompt: Which fluid do you order, and how?

choices.text: A balanced crystalloid in measured portions, reassessing after each.
choices.feedback: In shock, give volume quickly in measured portions and reassess after each. The type matters less than the amount: SMART found a small kidney signal favoring balanced crystalloids (14.3% versus 15.4%), and Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2012 recommends vasopressors together with fluids in vasomotor shock (1C). Reassess perfusion after each portion, and call the attending about a vasopressor if the pressure stays low.
choices.then: By 02:00, after 2.5 liters, he responds without a vasopressor.

choices.text: 0.9% saline in measured portions, reassessing perfusion after each.
choices.feedback: Acceptable. In the double-blind BaSICS and PLUS trials, 90-day death did not differ between saline and a balanced solution; saline is appropriate when it is the fluid in stock. Large volumes add chloride, so watch the bicarbonate.

choices.text: 5% dextrose in water, run fast, since it is the fluid already hanging at the bedside.
choices.feedback: The glucose is metabolized and leaves free water, which spreads into every compartment, mostly into cells, and adds very little to the plasma. It does not resuscitate and can drop the sodium.
choices.then: The nurse questions the order. You change it to a crystalloid in measured portions; by 02:00, after 2.5 liters, he responds.

choices.text: 4% albumin first, because it stays inside the vessels and so needs less volume.
choices.feedback: In sepsis the capillary barrier leaks and albumin’s advantage shrinks. SAFE found no difference in death at 28 days, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2012 suggests isotonic crystalloids rather than colloids (2B), and the family pays for albumin out of pocket.
choices.then: You switch to a crystalloid in measured portions; by 02:00, after 2.5 liters, he responds.

n2.scene: On the ward, Mr. Agustin is alert and warm, on 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula. His cumulative balance is +4.2 liters. His urine output has been about 25 mL an hour for four hours, just under 0.5 mL/kg per hour. The nurse asks Dr. Soriano for a fluid bolus.

choices.text: Give a bolus: the urine output is below 0.5 mL/kg per hour.
choices.feedback: Urine output falls in acute kidney injury (AKI) from any cause, not only from low volume. He is warm, alert and well perfused, so a low urine output on its own is not a reason for fluid.
choices.then: Before it runs, you examine him and do a quick ultrasound instead.

choices.text: Start furosemide to protect the kidneys and push the urine out.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2012 recommends not using diuretics to prevent AKI (1B). A diuretic removes salt and water from a patient who has too much; it does not repair the kidney.
choices.then: You cancel it, examine him, and do a quick ultrasound.

choices.text: Answer in writing: he is perfused; no reflex bolus; test responsiveness and tolerance first.
choices.feedback: Perfusion, responsiveness and tolerance are separate questions. Healthy people are fluid responsive too, so responsiveness alone is no reason to give fluid, and a leg raise watched only by blood pressure is a weak test. A passive leg raise only if output can be measured in real time; look at the lungs and inferior vena cava (IVC) for tolerance.
choices.then: Lung ultrasound shows B-lines only over the pneumonia; the IVC is 1.8 cm and collapses partly. No bolus. The maintenance fluid continues “until he eats.”

choices.text: No bolus for now; recheck the urine output at the end of the shift and call if it stays low.
choices.feedback: The right restraint, but no assessment and no stop point. Write down whether he is perfused, responsive and tolerant, so the next person does not simply give the bolus.
choices.then: You return to examine him and do a quick ultrasound. The maintenance fluid continues “until he eats.”

vitals.iv: Maintenance at admission rate + antibiotic carriers

n3.scene: Day three. His fever is gone and he finished his rice porridge. He is breathing 26 times a minute with a saturation of 91% on 2 liters, and you hear new crackles at both bases. On the ward standing scale he weighs 65.5 kg. Ultrasound shows B-lines in both lungs, small effusions, and an IVC of 2.4 cm with little variation. The maintenance fluid is still running at the rate written on Sunday, and his antibiotics run in their own carrier bags. His creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL.
n3.prompt: Dr. Soriano asks what to change this morning.

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus, because the creatinine is rising.
choices.feedback: Congestion raises venous pressure, and the kidney in its capsule loses perfusion pressure and filters less. More fluid for a rising creatinine in a congested patient tightens the cycle.
choices.then: His saturation falls to 88%. You stop the bolus and the maintenance fluid.

choices.text: Name the phase as evacuation: stop maintenance fluid, count carriers, propose fluid removal.
choices.feedback: A positive balance on day three is a decision someone forgot to make. He eats, he is perfused, and he is congested: the fluid has no job, and fluid creep from carriers adds to it. Concentrate the drug infusions and propose fluid removal to the attending with a daily goal.

choices.text: Halve the maintenance rate and reassess tomorrow, once the creatinine trend is clearer.
choices.feedback: Better, but still fluid with no job in a patient who eats and is congested. A large IVC alone does not mean too much fluid, but with crackles, B-lines, effusions and a rising weight, it does.
choices.then: At noon his saturation is 90%. You stop the maintenance fluid and count the carriers.

choices.text: Switch the maintenance from saline to a balanced crystalloid at the same rate.
choices.feedback: The trials found small or no differences between the bags and large harms from too much of any of them. The problem is the volume, not the chloride.
choices.then: You stop the maintenance fluid and count the carriers.

n4.scene: The attending agrees: his perfusion is stable, so a diuretic trial can start, with the drug and dose per the unit’s formulary.
n4.prompt: What do you write so the team can tell whether it is working?

choices.text: Strict urine output: it is working if the urine bag fills, so record the volume every hour.
choices.feedback: Volume alone can mislead: a large urine volume with little sodium removes water but little of the extracellular excess. Measure the sodium as well, knowing that natriuresis is a surrogate.
choices.then: You add a spot urine sodium after the dose, a daily goal, weight and laboratory checks.

vitals.order: Net negative goal; urine Na after dose; daily weight and labs

choices.text: A daily net negative goal, urine sodium after the dose, same-scale weights, daily electrolytes.
choices.feedback: The response is measured in sodium, not only in milliliters. In PUSH-AHF, natriuresis-guided therapy raised sodium excretion without changing death or readmission, so treat urine sodium as a guide, not a goal in itself. The goal is agreed with the attending; check potassium, magnesium and creatinine daily.

vitals.order: Net negative goal; urine Na after dose; daily weight and labs

choices.text: Diurese until the crackles are gone, and check laboratory values when the attending next rounds.
choices.feedback: Crackles are a late, insensitive sign, and the plan has no number and no stop point. Diuretics shift potassium and magnesium daily.
choices.then: You rewrite it with a daily goal, a urine sodium, weight and daily laboratory checks.

vitals.order: Net negative goal; urine Na after dose; daily weight and labs

n5.scene: After the first day of removal his net balance is −1.6 liters, he weighs 64.0 kg, and his saturation is 95% on room air with fewer crackles. His blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. His creatinine has risen from 1.7 to 1.9 mg/dL. Dr. Soriano is worried: “Should we stop and give fluid?”

choices.text: Continue the plan, tell the attending, and watch pressure and urine output.
choices.feedback: A modest creatinine rise during effective decongestion is common and often reflects changes in filtration pressure, not new tubular injury. Do not stop a working plan for a small rise without the attending, and do not continue it blindly if pressure or urine falls. Call if he becomes hypotensive or the urine output collapses.

vitals.order: Plan continued; attending informed of creatinine

choices.text: Stop the diuretic and give a bolus to bring the creatinine back down.
choices.feedback: His oxygen and weight are improving and his perfusion is fine. Refilling a patient who is still overloaded undoes the work and puts the lungs back at risk.
choices.then: You call the attending before acting; the plan continues with closer monitoring.

vitals.order: Plan continued; attending informed of creatinine

choices.text: Hold the diuretic until the creatinine returns to its baseline, then restart at a lower dose.
choices.feedback: Cautious, but it stops a working decongestion for a small rise that may not mean injury. Discuss it with the attending rather than stopping on your own.
choices.then: The attending asks you to continue with closer monitoring.

vitals.order: Plan continued; attending informed of creatinine

end.title: Saturday
end.text: Mr. Agustin is on room air, weighs 61.2 kg on the same standing scale, and his creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL. The diuretic stops at the agreed target. Dr. Soriano now writes the cumulative balance and the weight at the top of every progress note, and every fluid order on the ward carries its job and its stop point.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • In shock, give volume in measured portions and reassess. The type of crystalloid matters less than the amount; dextrose water does not resuscitate.
  • A low urine output is not, by itself, a reason for fluid. Ask three questions: perfused, responsive, tolerant.
  • Every fluid needs a job and a stop point. Maintenance running on day three in a patient who eats is a decision someone forgot to make.
  • Measure removal in sodium and weight, with a daily goal agreed with the attending.
  • A small creatinine rise during decongestion is discussed with the attending, not reflexively reversed; poor response despite escalation means a call about ultrafiltration or kidney replacement therapy.

See Where water goes, Assess honestly, Choose the fluid and Stop and remove.
